subject: Anatomy
summary: The vertebral column is a flexible, segmented structure that protects the spinal cord, supports the body, and allows movement. Its anatomy informs clinical decisions in trauma, infection, and degenerative disease.

sections.p: The vertebral column is a column of 33 vertebrae divided into cervical, thoracic, lumbar, sacral, and coccygeal regions. It balances structural rigidity with flexibility, protecting the spinal cord and enabling upright posture.
Each vertebra has a body, arch, and processes. Intervertebral discs provide cushioning. The column aligns with the pelvis and shoulders, forming the central axis of the body.
b: Body: weight bearing; arch: spinal cord passage; processes: muscle attachment

sections.p: Anteriorly the vertebral bodies lie beside the aorta, esophagus, and trachea. Posteriorly the spinal cord, nerve roots, and epidural fat are adjacent. The thoracic spine is tethered by ribs.
b: Anterior: great vessels, esophagus; Posterior: spinal cord, nerve roots

sections.p: Segmental arteries (vertebral, intercostal, lumbar) supply the vertebrae and discs. The venous plexus surrounds the spinal cord.
b: Vertebral artery: cervical; Intercostal: thoracic; Lumbar: lumbar

sections.p: The spinal cord exits through intervertebral foramina, giving rise to spinal nerves that innervate the body.
The column protects the spinal cord, supports the head and trunk, and allows flexion, extension, lateral bending, and rotation.
Trauma can cause fractures, dislocations, or spinal cord injury. Infections (TB, pyogenic) and malignancies can erode vertebrae, leading to pain and instability.
b: Fracture types: compression, burst, transverse; Infection: Pott disease; Malignancy: metastatic lesions

sections.p: Remember the red flags for spinal cord injury: loss of sensation below the lesion, motor weakness, bladder dysfunction. In low‑resource settings, a simple X‑ray and clinical exam can guide urgent care.
b: Red flags: sensory loss, motor deficit, bladder dysfunction

whenToSeekHelp: Loss of sensation below the waist
Sudden severe back pain with neurological deficit
Unexplained weight loss with back pain

faq.q: What is the most common type of spinal fracture in low‑resource settings?
faq.a: Compression fractures, often from osteoporosis or trauma, are most frequent.

faq.q: How does tuberculosis affect the vertebral column?
faq.a: Pott disease causes anterior vertebral body destruction, leading to kyphosis and potential spinal cord compression.

faq.q: When is surgical intervention indicated for a spinal fracture?
faq.a: When there is neurological deficit, instability, or progressive deformity.
